entries.title: Birdfy Nest Duo Review: My Own Private Nature Documentary
entries.summary: With two cameras and built-in climate sensors, the Birdfy Nest Duo let me watch an entire nesting season unfold.
entries.content:
Even though I've been a bird-watcher most of my life, nothing prepared me for the experience of witnessing—on my phone—the entire process of birds being born in my own backyard.

I’ve maintained a regular “dumb” nest box for years, the birthplace of generations of black-capped chickadees. I’ve seen them going in and out, but I always wondered what was happening in there, especially the year I opened up the box in the fall and found five deceased fledglings at the bottom. How could this have happened? I wondered.

Thanks to the Birdfy Nest Duo smart nesting box and its built-in thermometer and hygrometer, I now at least have an educated guess. (The poor things likely overheated during an early season heat wave.) Being able to watch the entire nesting operation from all angles, starting with excavation and egg-laying and ending in hatching and fledging, has been one of the most educational and entertaining bird-watching experiences I have ever had, and something I'd recommend to anyone interested in birds, nature, or just life science in general.

Eye Spy

Birdfy makes three smart nest boxes in addition to the Duo. The original, the Birdfy Nest, has one camera—located inside the box—and can only hang from an eye hook screwed into the top. There's also a version made out of solid fir in contrast to the others’ lightweight bamboo. I have also tested Birdfy’s artful Polygon, but persistent connection issues prevented me from using it this season.

I have not tested the first two single-camera versions, but I can't imagine not having a second camera outside the hole to see who's unexpectedly poking their head in. (At one point in my testing, it was a confused flicker; another, a curious starling—this is when I learned chickadees can hiss). It's also critical to be able to pole-mount the box to keep it away from predators.

The Nest Duo is substantial—16 inches tall and about 8 pounds—with one 1080p HD camera facing the nest entry hole on the exterior and another tucked discreetly inside the nest box itself. There's also an internal hygrometer (humidity) and thermometer (temperature) that show readings on the live view in Birdfy's easy-to-use app. There are four easy-to-install, screw-on entry hole sizes for different species, from 0.9 inches for wrens up to 2 inches for starlings or bluebirds, along with corresponding metal predator guards to prevent chewing. The entire side of the box opens with a latch for easy cleaning and access.

In the app, each screen capture appears as a split-screen image, which you can tap to view 20-second videos (with audio) of both the inside and the outside of the box. The videos are immediately downloadable and shareable—no subscription is needed.

The screen captures work much like one of Birdfy's smart bird feeders, but with images shunted to sections labeled “Prelude,” “Nesting,” “Brooding,” “Nestling,” “Fledgling,” and “End.” There seemed to be no rhyme or reason for what process the app thought was happening at the time (for example, if a nestling was simply turned around, the app asked if it should label it as “Fledgling”), but this story format was easy enough to ignore onscreen.

House Hunters

In March of this year, at the beginning of nesting season on the West Coast, I installed the Duo with the 1-inch entry hole on a pole stand and mounted the included solar panel below the box with hose clamps. Black-capped chickadees were consistently interested, popping in and looking around, but something was preventing them from staking a claim. It took me a while to realize they were looking askance at the holes on the metal tray “floor,” which is perforated for drainage. The idea is that this tray can be inserted into one of a series of slots to increase or decrease the nest cavity depth, depending on your local species' preference.

entries.title: The Kindle Accessories I Never Want to Read Without (2026)
entries.summary: Looking to better protect your Kindle or add a little personality to your favorite e-reader? From cases and covers to page turners and even charms, this is the guide for you.
entries.content:
Your Kindle doesn't have to be just a plain e-reader. The right Kindle accessories can transform the simple device into something that showcases your personality, makes it easier to read, or all of the above. Personally, I'm always looking for a way to hold up one less device in front of my face; I'm holding my phone enough already, thank you very much.

If you're shopping around for new Kindle accessories, I've got you covered as a fellow reader and owner of every single current Kindle model. I've tried everything from clear cases you can fill with stickers to ones with built-in straps, and have tested straps you can add to your e-reader without needing a case. Stickers? Charms? Got ’em. Hate holding your Kindle up to read? The Kindle holders and page-turning remotes are for you. This guide will give you ideas on how to improve your own reading time or gift your favorite reader.

Updated August 2026: I've added a new section with compatible wall chargers and portable chargers, and updated pricing.

My Favorite Kindle Accessories

Kindle Cases and Covers

An easy must-have for any Kindle reader is a case or cover to protect your e-reader. Here are some of my favorites that I've tried on my various Kindles.

Kindle Straps and Grips

Looking for an easier way to hold your Kindle? Add these straps and grips right onto the Kindle or the case.

Kindle Holders

Hate holding up your Kindle? Or struggle with chronic pain that makes holding it feel terrible? These holders will literally take the weight out of your hands.

A Freestanding Charger

Looking to keep your Kindle charged without adding another cord to the floor of your desk or bedside table? Same. Here's a more stylish solution if you have one of the Signature editions.

More Charger Options

If you're getting a new Kindle, you might not be thrilled to discover you need to bring your own power base to charge it. And if you haven't already switched over your home's collection of wall chargers and bases to USB-C versions, you'll be especially frustrated when you open the box and find only a USB-C cord and port on the Kindle itself. If you're in the market for a new wall charger to pair with your Kindle, these are a couple of our favorites.

Looking to charge on the go? You shouldn't need to with a Kindle's long battery life. But in case you're a serial battery drainer, you can try these portable power banks we love. If neither of these suit you, check out our complete guide to the Best Power Banks.

A Kindle Page Turner

The hottest new item to get as a Kindle lover is a page turner. They're especially handy for holders like the ones above, where your hands aren't already on the device, and can make for a great accessibility accessory for readers with different needs.

My biggest irritation with these devices so far is that you have to charge them both individually, and if one runs out of battery, the whole thing is useless. I also don't love that the turner does tend to block at least one letter while I read, and you can't place it on the lower or upper margins since it'll activate the menus instead of turning the page. Still, it makes reading ultra comfortable, especially for my strained wrists.

Here's my favorite one so far, that's been solid at holding a charge, and next I'm testing this remote ($20) with a wearable ring clicker instead of a remote.

Kindle Adornments

While everything else in this guide serves a protective or convenience purpose, this section features items with a singular purpose: fun. Here are a few I've liked adding to my Kindle.

Kindle Bags and Sleeves

Looking for a bag to tote your Kindle around? These belt bags have you covered with a specific size and special pockets designed to safely store your device. Sure, you could throw your Kindle in any old bag, but these will keep it secure and prevent scratches from your keys. If you'd rather use the bag you have but want a separate sleeve to keep it safe, we've got ideas for that too.

Still Need a Kindle?

If you're reading this guide and actually are still in need of a Kindle, we've got an entire guide to the best Kindles to buy and why. Here are my top favorites.

FAQs

Can These Accessories Work With Other E-Readers, Like Kobo?

Some of them can! You'll have to check descriptions for certain items (like cases or things that have to perfectly fit the device) since other devices like Kobo and Nook don't have the same dimensions as a Kindle, but flexible straps, generic tablet holders, and decorative items like charms and stickers would easily work with any other e-reader you own.

entries.title: The Best Home Theater Projectors in 2026: XGIMI, Hisense, Leica, and More
entries.summary: Home theater projectors are getting better and better, and have quickly become my favorite way to enjoy movies.
entries.content:
I've seen some of the best movies and tested some of the best home projectors this year. Massively entertaining films like The Odyssey, Project Hail Mary, and Toy Story 5 have made 2026 a standout year for movies, and new home theater projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max and the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max have upped the game in terms of beautiful, cinematic, color-accurate images at home.

I've been reviewing the best TVs and projectors for years. That's why I put these latest home theater projectors to the test, running benchmarks to check for vividness, brightness, skin tone variations, and whether dark scenes look too washed out. I watched countless Netflix movies and 4K Blu-ray films—all for the cause. My main takeaway? These top models are giving the local cinema something to worry about. Bring some popcorn and a comfortable recliner, and you're basically there.

For more TV recommendations based on our expert testing, check out our related guides, including the Best RGB TVs, Best TVs, Best Large TVs, Best OLED TVs, and Best Cheap TVs. If you’re really undecided, read our guide on How to Buy the Right TV in 2026.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Best Overall

Picking the best projector was not easy, especially since there's so much competition. The Xgimi Titan Noir Max won me over because of the dynamic, self-adjusting iris. As you watch a movie or show, the projector adjusts to allow more light in (for bright scenes) or closes to reduce light (for dark scenes). For example, during a nighttime sequence in the movie Hoppers on Disney+, the iris will close to make the blacks and grays look dark and richly detailed. That feature alone sets the Titan Noir Max apart.

But it’s also highly capable in many other ways. It has an outstanding 10,000:1 native contrast ratio and a 7,000-lumen brightness rating, which helped it blast through all of my benchmarks and test scenarios. An early morning scene in the movie The Creator looked exactly like I would expect it to in real life, showing texture on the seaside cliffs. Even in a sun-drenched room, battle scenes in the movie War Machine looked bright and clear—outperforming the Hisense XR10 model.

More functionally, it has four adjustable feet that allow you to adjust the height or even set the projector on a side table and angle it toward a wall.

One downside is that, like many projectors, it doesn't natively run a streaming OS like Google TV, but I prefer to connect a Blu-ray player or Google TV Streamer anyway.

Specs
Refresh rate 240 Hz
Weight 18 pounds
HDMI ports 3
Light source Triple laser

Best for Gaming

I’ll never forget the first time I played the game 007 First Light projected on a wall in my house using the Hisense XR10. An ocean scene looked bright blue and realistic, thanks to the excellent color processing on this projector. I felt very little lag using the low-latency mode, and the built-in speakers (the best I've tested on a projector) never felt lacking.

The big and boxy XR10 is exactly what I would expect a high-end cinema projector to look like. It’s heavy at 23.4 pounds, but that’s because of its massive speaker and lens. Although I prefer the long adjustable legs on the Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the XR10 is stable and has a nicely subdued dark metallic look.

The iris is adjustable (in seven different ways) to allow more light in or to make darker scenes even more vivid. Games in particular looked rich and colorful, including one of my all-time favorites, Senua's Saga: Hellblade II. A beach scene had a texture and moodiness that was truly jaw-dropping.

I loved watching the movie Awake on Netflix, which is dark in almost every scene. (It was the first time I noticed a guy in the background of one scene wearing a blue shirt.) Most projectors render these dark scenes without enough contrast, but the XR10 makes them look stunning.

The XR10 is a monster of a home cinema projector, with only the Titan Noir Max performing just a bit better on color and brightness. And you do need to adjust the iris manually in the settings, though (unlike the automatic adjustments of the Titan Noir Max).

Specs
Refresh rate 240 Hz
Weight 23 pounds
HDMI ports 3
Light source Triple laser

Best for Movies

Leica has a rich history making cameras, and this Leica Cine Play 1 projector is a showcase of that superior craftsmanship. The Leica Summicron lens renders ultra-realistic video with extreme clarity and exceptional color accuracy. I watched Hoppers in a windowless testing room, and the furry creatures all looked stunningly realistic—you could even see individual strands of fur cleanly.

That’s why I think it's the best projector for movies and shows. Colors pop on the screen like you are watching in a theater. This model exceeds the BT.2020 color gamut spec by 107 percent, and you can tell in movies like Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. In one segment, the reds and blues looked even more vivid than I remembered at the theater.

The compact size (about the same as a large lunch box) and good portability (weighing about 15 pounds) were two highlights for me. I also like the metallic design with the iconic red Leica logo on top. The projector can easily sit on a table, or you can add the Cine Play 1 Floor Stand for $495. The power cord connects to the base of the stand, which makes for a very clean setup.

It's impressive, but not as impressive in a bright room, unfortunately—this projector is best utilized at night. And it lacks the dynamic iris of the Titan Noir Max (which is, admittedly, much pricier).

Specs
Refresh rate 120 Hz
Weight 15 pounds
HDMI ports 2
Light source Triple laser

Best Budget

I had to double check the price of the BenQ W4100i because it's so much cheaper than my other top picks. Yet, of all the home cinema projectors I've tested in the last few months, the quick and easy setup on this model, plus a few unusual perks, made it a top pick.

It's easy to configure, even though it uses the older Android TV operating system. I asked the onboard Google Assistant bot to start the install process and it only took a few minutes to do the whole thing. While the dark gray enclosure is understated, I liked how easy it was to adjust the focus and throw distance using analog levers on the top of the projector.

At this price, the W4100i is not meant to compete with the titans of home cinema like the Hisense XR10, and it matches an older color gamut spec (Rec.709). The lumens rating is only 3,200, far below the Titan Noir Max's 7,000.

Still, there are a few interesting perks with the BenQ W4100i. It has a mode that can match the 24p frame rate of movies for a more fluid look. With the refresh rate cranked to 240 Hz, playing the game NTE on my gaming laptop, I came to realize just how much I like using this projector for low-latency gaming. My controller flicks were rendered immediately during chaotic battle scenes.

I’m not sure why BenQ insists on still using a dongle attachment for the operating system. You can skip it altogether if you use one of the HDMI ports for a Blu-ray player or another device. In the end, the lower-than-expected price, low latency, and easy setup are what sold me on this BenQ.

Specs
Refresh rate 240 Hz
Weight 22 pounds
HDMI ports 2
Light source LED

Honorable Mentions

Epson Lifestudio Grand Plus for $3,800: A powerhouse for movies and shows, this short-throw projector can be set right next to your projector screen or blank wall and display a huge image. It also, surprisingly, has Google Gemini built in, which can do some surprising tasks like create slideshows, fit with animations, original images, voice-overs, and more.

AWOL Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector for $4,449: I’m currently in the middle of testing this short-throw model, and it is an engineering marvel. The incredible 6000:1 contrast ratio and triple-laser light source are just the beginning. I’ve been impressed by the color accuracy, brightness, deep blacks, and extreme clarity across the entire image.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why Use a Home Theater Projector?

It’s an eternal debate—should you pull the shades, fire up a home theater projector, and watch a movie like you’re at the local cineplex? Or is it better to use a massive OLED or RGB television that will show a clearer image during a sunny day? Here’s my take after testing tons of the latest projectors and TVs: I prefer projectors for movies because I can max out the screen size to 120 inches or more. There’s just nothing like watching a 12-foot projected image of a movie with Dolby Atmos surround sound at home.

What Do You Need to Use a Home Theater Projector?

The short answer is quite simple: You just need a white wall. Purists will say a true home cinema experience requires a projector screen and a windowless room, and I have a testing room just for that purpose. However, all of the models I’m recommending are so bright and colorful that they perform quite well on a large wall without needing a projector screen. I do recommend room-darkening shades, though, because a darker room does create a better image.

Why Are Home Theater Projectors So Expensive?

Consumer-grade home theater projectors cost around $3,000 or more. In my experience, the latest large OLED and RGB televisions can easily cost just as much. I strongly recommend sticking to the $3,000 price point for a home cinema projector, though, because many midrange models (e.g., under $2,000) don’t look that colorful or bright. They also suffer from some serious contrast problems. For serious movie and TV fans, I’d avoid projectors that cost less than $1,000.

entries.title: Forget Meta Ray-Bans. These Dorky-Looking Virtual Display Glasses Are Way More Useful
entries.summary: Tethered display glasses are truly practical face computers. They trade bulky spatial computing for simplicity: Plug in, recline, and get a massive screen right in front of your nose.
entries.content:
“URGENT: Immediate Action Required” blasts into my eyeballs as I scroll through the impossibly giant email inbox looming directly in front of my face.

I’m reclined way back in a chair, wearing a pair of Xreal smart glasses. Tethered to my laptop via a USB-C cord, these glasses mirror the laptop screen and project it into a virtual display. The virtual screen is gigantic, equivalent to a 170-inch TV that feels about a foot away from my nose. I’m the only one who can see it, and so I’ve got this massive display all to myself.

With this technological marvel, I conjure the most riveting view imaginable: five workplace training modules about business principles and cybersecurity that my boss has repeatedly reminded me are very overdue. The text on the screen is blurry, but I complete them all within my virtual display. It takes several hours. By the time I’m done, the glasses have overheated, my forehead is sweaty, and I’m still not sure I can actually recognize a phishing email.

Virtual display glasses are a much more niche category of mixed-reality smart glasses than the camera-equipped, AI-powered frames that have dominated the product market—namely, Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses. Made by companies like Xreal, Viture, and Rokid, these glasses aim to bring a screen directly to your face. Like a portable monitor, plug the USB-C cable into the arm of the glasses, then stick the other end into the port of just about any laptop, phone, tablet, or handheld gaming console. Slap ’em on, and that screen mirrors in a holographic VR-style projection, right in your center of vision.

Wearing them, you can chill out in an airplane seat, lie prone, even dangle upside-down if you like, and the big screen stays right there with you. (No tech neck!) Yup, you're basically cosplaying the lazy humans in Wall-E. Hooray.

Virtual display glasses don’t get the heat of privacy issues that Meta’s “pervert glasses” do. No cameras, no recording—just sweet, sweet content consumption beamed out an inch from your eye holes. If you're feeling generous, the Xreal glasses could even be lauded for their privacy protections, at least for the user. Got sensitive documents or embarrassing videos you're trying to watch on a plane? A virtual display is one only the wearer can see. (The Xreal glasses also have speakers in the frames that do leak sound, so be careful with your audible content consumption.)

Display-only glasses make good on at least one promise made by other wearable mixed-reality devices. When Apple launched its flawed Vision Pro headset, one of its primary features was spatial computing that let you work and watch entertainment in a virtual workspace. But the device was too heavy and bulky to wear for long. Xreal’s specs are much simpler and less elegant but do accomplish most of that goal in a much lighter package. (We’ve also had a pretty great experience with Sightful’s Spacetop spatial computing interface, also powered by Xreal glasses.)

“The fundamental thing these glasses do well is that they just work,” says Anshel Sag, a principal analyst at the industry advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategies. Sag says he wears these kinds of glasses regularly on flights. “You plug them in, and you have faith that you're going to get a video signal on those glasses that mostly matches what's on the screen of the device they're plugged into.”

I’ve been swapping between two of the glasses. First, Xreal’s $849 ROG Xreal R1, available to preorder and expected to ship in September. It displays that 171-inch virtual screen in a 57-degree field of view, which you can anchor in place or have the screen stay dead center in your vision as you turn your head different directions.

I've also used the much cheaper, much lighter Xreal xbx A01+, which the company launched in May and started shipping in July. It costs $299 but has a smaller screen with a 50-degree field of view. It has less of a heat issue but also lower screen quality. Crucially, you can't anchor the screen, which can make watching stuff disorienting when the screen moves every time your head does.

Xreal’s primary selling point for these glasses is gaming or watching videos. The glasses don’t use batteries and instead sip power from your plugged-in device. I’ve connected both frames to my Steam Deck and blasted through seas of demons in Diablo IV on a giant virtual screen. I tried watching the extended editions of the Lord of the Rings films, but I had plugged the device into my phone, which died halfway through the first movie. I’ve also plugged the glasses into my laptop for regular browsing, lurking on social media, and being a nuisance in my workplace Slack.

The glasses don’t work with everything. I tried connecting them to my PlayStation 5, which required a much longer cord and more patience than I can muster in return for a not-so-great display across my vision.

The very stern faces of actors portraying harassment victims in my workplace training videos have an almost 3D-ified quality, their pouting chins jutting out past the blocks of text. The animations in this very good WIRED story hit way harder than they did on my lil’ laptop screen. Unfortunately, the smaller text in the article was almost too blurry to read.

Virtual displays still don’t have the resolution and fidelity that we’re used to on our laptops and smartphones. They tend to be fuzzy, and I almost feel like it’s a simulation of what it would be like to need a glasses prescription. After staring at that virtual screen for hours, I pop it off, and it feels like I’ve had my eyes crossed for too long and they’re ready to stay that way.

The glasses also aren’t exactly inconspicuous enough for me to feel comfortable walking around in them. You can pop off the projection lenses and wear them like regular glasses, but you probably won’t, because they look very chunky and won’t fool anyone. As I used them in the office, I asked a nearby coworker if I looked cool wearing them. She just laughed.

So the Xreal glasses aren’t perfect. They certainly aren’t something I want to wear all that long. But they are good enough at what they do to offer a glimpse of a smart glasses ecosystem coming into focus. They also seem to be growing in popularity. Tech analyst firm International Data Corporation wrote in a report that virtual monitor glasses, like Xreal and Viture, “represent the fastest-growing segment” of the smart glasses market. IDC projects them selling around 3 million units in 2026. That's a small part of the same projection that puts sales of all smart glasses at nearly 14 million units in 2026, but it ain’t nothing.

Xreal also has bigger ambitions that will take its products into another category of XR glasses—the ones with cameras and recording capabilities, though they’re still not designed to be something you wear walking about. Xreal’s Project Aura, a partnership with Google running on the Android XR platform, will launch later this year. All of Xreal’s efforts have been leading to this.

“These are a means to an end, and that end is Project Aura,” Sag says. He doesn’t think the existence of the Aura glasses—expected to cost under $1,500—spells the end of Xreal’s other offerings. “You have to be able to create access points for people at different prices,” Sag says. “And that's why I think these glasses will continue to exist, because you have to ramp people up to making a purchase over a thousand dollars.”

entries.title: The Best Multiuse Air Purifier for Home in 2026: BlueAir, Rabbit Air, Dreame
entries.summary: These WIRED-tested dual-purpose air purifiers also function as heaters, fans, art pieces, and more, offering the best of both worlds.
entries.content:
If you're tight on space or just want a more aesthetically pleasing machine, the best air purifier for home depends on your needs.

If you live in a small apartment like me, you may need to have a multifunctional air purifier for a practical reason: space. These compact, dual-purpose machines are useful if you are tight on square footage or don't want to shell out the money for two separate appliances. Or maybe you're aesthetically driven and want something that looks cool in your space rather than a clunky, large air purifier that can be an eyesore.

Regardless of the reason, these multiuse air purifiers look good, save space, and combine appliances into a single, energy-efficient device.

Check out our other home air quality guides, including the Best Fans, Best Space Heaters, Best Humidifiers, Best Dehumidifiers, and Best Window ACs.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Featured in This Guide

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Fan

This Dreo offers 99.97 percent HEPA filtration and an air quality sensor. You can control it with a remote, the Dreo app, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. Best of all, the fan and purifier can operate independently, in case you need just one or the other or want to extend the filter lifespan (replacements run around $40). The 12-month warranty isn’t the greatest, but the device has been trouble-free for nearly two years in our long-term tests. If you're in the market for a fan and purifier in one, this model is definitely worth a look. —Kat Merck

Smart app Yes (compatible with Alexa and Google Home)
Remote Yes
Ideal room size 100 square feet to achieve 4.5 air changes per hour
Weight 17.8 pounds
Noise on high 62 dB (if both air purifier and fan are on max settings)
Filter Prefilter, HEPA
Warranty 1-year limited
Extra Features Doubles as a fan; air purifier and fan can work independently of each other

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Heater

Blueair’s small-room model is a little under 2 feet tall and has built-in heating and cooling. Blueair’s app is easy to use, and I preferred it rather than the actual control panel. The panel did not always illuminate when pressed, making the buttons difficult to use. The app also has more options, like controlling the oscillation speed and angle. Blueair uses both mechanical HEPA filtration and electrostatic technology to capture pollutants in the air. Its CARB certification is listed as electronic, unlike HEPA-only air purifiers that are listed as mechanical.

The ComfortPure 3-in-1 also has an air quality index indicator light that responds to the purifier's built-in sensor to measure particulate matter (PM) 2.5. The easy-to-miss sliver of light glows blue for excellent, green for good, yellow for moderate, orange for polluted, and red for very polluted. It has a control panel lock and filter change indicator light. I also appreciate the cloth handle that makes moving the Blueair easy. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Smart app Yes
Remote Yes
Ideal room size 200 sq ft to achieve four air exchanges per hour
Weight 13.5 lbs
Noise on high 53 dB
Filter Activated carbon, HEPA
Warranty 1 year, 3 years with registration
Extra Features Doubles as a fan and heater

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Vacuum

The Eye-Vac Air combines an air purifier with a touchless vacuum. Sweep debris up to the stationary unit, and it'll suck it up. It has two sets of HEPA and activated carbon filters pulling in air from both sides of the purifier. Its filter placement lets you position the Eye-Vac flush against the wall, which is especially useful in kitchen settings. The air filter can clean the air effectively, achieving five air exchanges per hour in a 120-square-foot space. While the large control panel is easy to read, the air purifier and vacuum offer only two options: manual or automatic. Indicator lights show when the bagless vacuum canister is full and when the air purifier filters need replacing. There are three fan speeds, but there are no color-coded indicator lights that correspond to air quality. Instead, three blue bars indicate the fan setting. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Smart app No
Remote No
Ideal room size 120 square feet to achieve 5 air exchanges per hour
Weight 13 pounds
Noise on high 53 dB (85 dB for vacuum)
Filter HEPA, activated carbon

Best Air Purifier That Doubles as Art

After testing a dozen or so air purifiers in my tiny apartment, I realized what an eyesore they can be. This air purifier doubles as art and, at the very least, a conversation piece. With such little space, I generally want my tech to be multifunctional, or at the very least look good. When my mom visited, she thought the MinusA2 was an art TV or a monitor with an art background, until it auto-engaged and ran on high after the Canadian wildfire smoke reached New York this summer. This air purifier comes in several artwork styles, including Monet's Water Lilies and Van Gogh's Starry Night, and can be easily hung flush against the wall by removing the bottom stand and using the included mounting bracket.

You can also customize the six-layer filter system inside, with options for a pet allergy-specific filter (which I opted for), germ defense for viruses and bacteria, a charcoal-enhanced odor remover, and a toxin absorber that reduces formaldehyde, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and harmful chemicals. Along with the custom filter, there is a reusable, washable prefilter; a medium filter for pollen and mold; a HEPA filter; an activated carbon filter for odor control; and a negative ion generator. The filters should last up to two years on average if the unit runs for 12 hours a day and is cleaned regularly. I didn't love that it doesn't have wheels or a handle, but it can be easily mounted if you'd rather display it off the floor. It was also super quiet, even on the highest fan speeds. With the remote or the buttons on the unit, you can change fan speeds or pick settings like auto, sleep, or pollen mode. On the front, there's also an odor sensor and light indicating air quality.

Best Air Purifier That’s Also a Sunrise Alarm Clock

The Mini Restful is part of Blueair’s Sleep Collection, and is nearly the smallest air purifier I’ve tested. My sound level meter registered 60 dB—around the sound of a conversation. No one is sleeping with that noise—the Mini Restful is only quiet on its lowest setting. The sunrise alarm clock feature was easy to program through Blueair’s app, and it has nine sounds to choose from, like Midnight Rain, Happy Rise, and Mantra Breeze. entries.title: They Dedicated Their Lives to Teaching. Then the Deepfakes Started
entries.summary: The deepfake epidemic in schools is affecting more than students. Four teachers tell WIRED about becoming targets of sexualized, AI-generated content—and how difficult it was to find accountability.
entries.content:
For Luis DeSantiago, a substitute teacher in Los Banos, California, it started with a few text messages. On March 12, as he was working his other part-time job at a coffee shop, his phone lit up. A fellow barista said there was an AI photo circulating on social media. Her cousin wanted to know if it was DeSantiago.

At first, DeSantiago wasn’t worried—he figured that inappropriate photos violated TikTok’s community guidelines and were usually quickly removed.

“When I finally saw the image, that’s when it felt like a punch to the gut,” DeSantiago tells WIRED. Parts of it resembled a mirror selfie that he remembered taking at a job in college. But instead of his work uniform, he was wearing lingerie. And instead of standing normally, as he had been in the original photo, he was posing suggestively.

The texts kicked off a monthslong saga that crossed two schools and involved students and administrators. And DeSantiago is far from the only educator who’s been victimized this way.

WIRED spoke with three other teachers who allege that their students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI. They say the incidents have been profoundly distressing and disappointing—and in some cases, it’s led them to reassess how they view their work and their relationships with their students.

“This Could Include Other Students”

After he received the texts, DeSantiago began to piece together who might have been behind the image. One account that shared it used their real name in their TikTok profile—it was a student DeSantiago knew from the local middle school, where he regularly filled in. DeSantiago suspected the involvement of two other students based on people who followed and interacted with that account, and his knowledge of student friend groups. He was scheduled to work at that very middle school the next day.

DeSantiago reported the incident to the assistant principal, who assured him that the school would "take care of it.” Later that evening, he decided to look for the image by searching his name on TikTok. He discovered that a different student had created an account impersonating him—it used his name, slightly mispelled, and had the same photo as their profile picture.

Over the next few weeks, DeSantiago says, he went back and forth with school administrators, the parents of the students, and even the police.

“If these students aren't afraid of generating and posting these images of me, I am concerned of what they may be circulating privately through text messages and group chats,” DeSantiago wrote to the principal. “Keep in mind this could include other students as well.”

One student, who admitted to creating the image, was disciplined with in-school suspension. DeSantiago was later told that the image was also shared on Snapchat. But DeSantiago says the image continued to proliferate, and other students began posting it. He says he also received several crude, sexual comments on his TikTok account.

DeSantiago told administrators he didn’t want to take assignments at the middle school “until this matter is fully addressed.” The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

He took a substitute assignment at the local high school, but the problems followed him. During one class, he received an AirDropped photo of the same AI-generated image before it was quickly revoked. He could tell it was circulating among the class.

The principal told him the school was launching an “immediate investigation” and offered to meet with DeSantiago or make the school counselor available, but DeSantiago says he probably won’t return to the district this year.

He tells WIRED that, at least right now, he doesn’t feel safe doing so.

“It Makes You Question Everything”

When fake nude images of nonconsenting adults are disseminated, it could constitute cyberstalking and violate the federal Take It Down Act, which makes it a crime to publish nonconsensual “intimate visual depictions of individuals, both authentic and computer-generated,” on the internet.

In most of the accounts shared with WIRED, the teachers didn't directly report the content to the platforms on which it appeared. Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy shared the company's policies on harassment and sexual content, which prohibit sharing AI-generated or manipulated content to humiliate or sexually harass others. She told WIRED that the company has "established processes" for reporting such content, and that it continues to "develop features and tools designed to support the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." TikTok did not provide comment before publication.

Donna Ballman, a retired employment advocacy lawyer, tells WIRED that if a student creates and shares sexual images of a teacher, it constitutes a “clear case” of sexual harassment in the workplace.

Ballman says that under federal antidiscrimination laws, employers have an obligation to create a workplace free of sexual harassment. In a school, this could mean disciplining the student or moving them to a different classroom. She adds, however, that there's “no blueprint” for how schools need to respond to these incidents. Administrators don’t even have to tell a victimized teacher how a student may have been disciplined.

“They just have to make [and] create a safe environment for the victim,” Ballman says.

One middle school teacher in her mid-twenties tells WIRED that she’s seen so much AI-generated content used to harass teachers that she’s bracing for the next wave. (She requested anonymity because she did not have permission from her school district to speak about her experience.)

Last year, she says, students found public photos of a teacher in her sixties, manipulated them to make it appear that she was committing sex acts, and shared them with each other in a Snapchat group chat.

A few months ago, the teacher says, she learned from a student about a TikTok account impersonating her. It looked AI-generated—her face had the characteristic smoothness of AI-generated content, her mouth was moving unnaturally while speaking, and the sound of her voice didn’t match her own. Some of the videos showed her doing things like skydiving or backflips. But others depicted her talking about sexual acts she performed and enjoyed.

She says she told her principal about the account and that they assured her that they would “see what we can do.” Throughout the day, students continued to warn her about the account. She says that some told her that they knew who made the account—one of their classmates. She says the student was known to have behavioral problems.

“I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me genuinely believed that was my account, and that I was saying those things,” she tells WIRED. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, you guys—that is not me.’” She asked them to report it to TikTok, and she says the account was quickly taken down.

Still unnerved by the incident, she mentioned the TikTok account during the next monthly teacher meeting. A colleague said he had seen a seemingly AI-generated fake video of himself getting arrested, which he believed was generated by the same student.

As days and weeks passed, she says, she became the target of escalating, in-person harassment from this same student, who began “cursing me out, calling me names, telling me to fuck off, calling me a bitch.” She raised it at the next faculty meeting, and the assistant principal said that the same student was calling and texting them in the middle of the night and posting apparent AI-generated photos of them to TikTok.

She says the principal removed the student from her class and tried to limit his access to her. But she says that the harassment continued until the student ultimately left the district, and TikTok removed the account.

She says that these behavioral issues aren’t exclusive to this particular student. “It's kind of unsurprising that we are dealing with that, because these kids just have a hard time,” she says. "I'm just worried about this happening again.”

Other teachers say their experiences have fundamentally changed the way they relate to students.

Alice, who asked to be identified by her first name, works for a UK college that trains students aged 16 to 19 in trades like construction. Her job combines administrative responsibilities, like taking attendance, with the role of a college counselor. She says she individually meets with about 150 students throughout the year and takes pride in being able to be a sounding board, give them advice, and serve as a mentor.

This winter, she says, school administrators told her that a student filed a report claiming two videos were circulating among his classmates. One appeared to be real, and it showed her having a conversation with a student. The other one, they said, appeared to be a manipulated version of the first. But instead of talking to the student, it showed her taking her clothes off and dancing around in what was either underwear or a bikini.

Alice tells WIRED that as a qualified youth worker, part of her job often involves talking about things that students may feel “too embarrassed to tell their parents about,” like drugs, parties, or having safe sex. She says she had several of those conversations with the student she suspected had created the video. The student denied it when questioned by administrators and soon dropped out of the school. (The college did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

“It makes me reflect as well on those conversations, thinking, did he think that he could overstep a line because we were having these discussions?” she says. “It makes you question everything,” she says.

Afterward, the college gave her permission to step away from the class for a few weeks and took steps to educate students about the danger of creating or distributing deepfakes. But when she returned, she says, the atmosphere had chilled.

“I did have a really good rapport with my students—I do have a good rapport with my students,” she says. And she still loves her work. “But it's definitely made me a bit more cautious, a bit more vigilant when it comes to folks.”

“It Crosses the Line”

Like DeSantiago, Arizona-based sixth-grade teacher Luke Red says his students circulated an AI-generated photo of him in the comments of his public TikTok account. The image depicted him and another male teacher kissing each other.

Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok—not for content violations but for being under the minimum age of 13—but says TikTok didn’t remove the accounts. He says that the school immediately launched an investigation and quickly identified the student, who admitted to creating and sharing the image. The student received a three-day suspension—the most severe punishment kids their age can receive for a first-time sexual harassment offense, according to the school district handbook. The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Red tells WIRED that reflecting on the experience “has kind of sent me into a spiral.” His concerns, he says, are not necessarily about what happened to him. They’re more focused on the enthusiastic, permissive culture surrounding AI use among his students.

“It just got to the point where students felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images,” Red says. “Obviously when you're making your teachers do sexual things with these images, that's where it crosses the line.”

Ultimately, he feels more sorry for the students than for himself.

“It's just clear [that] so many kids nowadays just don't understand not only how what they're doing can affect others, but just what happens on the internet and how dangerous it can be,” Red says.

entries.title: NASA’s New Space Telescope Is Poised to Discover Hidden Facets of the Universe
entries.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is expected to discover as many as 200,000 new planets and reveal details about the elusive nature of dark matter and dark energy.
entries.content:
Astronomers have known for decades that an invisible substance permeates the cosmos. Detected only by its gravitational influence on visible objects, dark matter accounts for some 85 percent of all matter, enveloping entire galaxies in great spheroids that branch and interweave to form the scaffolding of the universe.

But the specifications of this grand architecture remain shrouded in mystery. Driven by a ghostly force that scientists call dark energy, the universe is ever-changing, constantly expanding at an accelerating rate.

A new space telescope, launching as soon as August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, will attempt to untangle the nature of these dark intergalactic phenomena. With the resolution of Hubble and a field of view about 100 times as big, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide a new way to look at the universe that could help solve some of the biggest questions in astrophysics.

“An observatory like Roman is intrinsically a discovery machine,” says Julie McEnery, NASA’s senior project scientist for the space telescope. “We're going to find rare things, unusual things, new things, surprising things.”

During its five-year primary mission, Roman will map expansive swaths of space to develop a comprehensive picture of galaxies and dark matter, helping scientists understand how the universe’s largest formations change over time. The telescope, named for the first chief astronomer of NASA, will trace astrophysical structures by measuring subtle distortions of light caused by gravity, allowing scientists to study how dark energy is driving cosmic evolution.

“We’re not measuring the property of something in the universe,” McEnery says of this work. “We’re understanding how the universe we’re in fundamentally works.”

Roman’s sharp, wide view is also expected to capture as many as 200,000 new planets, an extraordinary leap from the roughly 6,300 confirmed exoplanets. The telescope will spot most of these worlds as they block some of the light from their host stars, but its high sensitivity will allow it to detect an additional 1,000 or so by measuring the planets’ gravitational effects on starlight.

Given the space telescope’s powerful resolution and wide area of study, there’s no telling exactly what else it may find.

“The most exciting science from Roman,” McEnery says, “may well be something that we can't even imagine now.”

Whole New Worlds

In many ways, Roman will be a partner to the James Webb Space Telescope. Both primarily observe infrared light, and like Webb, Roman will orbit a point in space nearly a million miles away from Earth called Lagrange Point 2, where the telescopes can effectively block out light from the sun, Earth, and moon.

But where Webb is designed to peer deep into the cosmos, Roman will take a wide view.

“If we consider what the James Webb Space Telescope is doing, it's optimized towards looking at the very distant universe … but just a tiny patch of the sky,” says astrophysicist Rachel Mandelbaum of Carnegie Mellon University. “In contrast, Roman is able to look at a large area of the sky at once.”

That broad view will allow Roman to scour hundreds of millions of stars in search of planets. Similar to previous missions, the space observatory will find most of its targets by looking for planets that transit in front of their host stars. This is a highly effective technique to find large planets with short orbits, but to look for different kinds of worlds, Roman will use another trick called microlensing.

When two stars line up one in front of the other, the light from the background star is warped and magnified by the gravity of the star in the foreground. If that foreground star happens to host a planet, Roman will be able to detect how the planet’s gravity further magnifies the starlight coming from behind.

“This method can detect planets that are farther away from their stars than other methods,” says Matthew Penny, an exoplanet researcher at Louisiana State University. “You don't need the planet to complete an entire orbit before you see it.”

Roman is so sensitive to these microlensing effects that it should be able to detect planets with less mass than Mercury. It will also have the ability to spot free-floating “rogue” planets that have been cast away from their stars or that formed alone in the void.

By studying these new populations of planets, scientists can learn more about the conditions that may produce a system like our own and, by extension, a life-bearing planet like Earth.

“Our solar system is potentially quite unique, although we don't really know at this point,” Penny says. “There's a lot of potentially lucky coincidences in the solar system that make life possible.”

Probing the outer regions of planetary systems will provide key missing pieces to this puzzle. For example, the formation of large planets farther from a star may allow smaller planets to form closer in, Penny says, near the habitable zone where liquid water could form.

“Without a complete census of the whole range of possible planets, we don't really know how common planets like Earth are,” Penny says, “or planetary systems like our own.”

The Dark Universe

In addition to many new worlds, Roman’s gaze will fall upon more than a billion galaxies. In particular, it will focus on a population of galaxies between about 2 billion and 6 billion years after the Big Bang.

“One of the things that we try to study is the history and growth of cosmic structure,” Mandelbaum says. “In the very early universe, the matter was almost uniformly distributed. But there were tiny perturbations or tiny regions that were just a fraction more dense or less dense.”

Those slightly denser regions attracted more and more material over time, eventually forming immense clumps of dark matter that scientists call halos. Gas was then driven to the center of these dark matter haloes, where it ignited stars that swirled together to form galaxies.

Roman will create an extraordinarily detailed map of visible galaxies, and it will map the distribution of dark matter with more precision than ever before using a technique called weak gravitational lensing.

“Anytime we have a light ray from one galaxy that has to pass through the universe, including all kinds of structures, to us, the path of that light ray is getting slightly perturbed,” Mandelbaum says.

By comparing those perturbed light rays from many galaxies, scientists can trace the cosmic web of dark matter that surrounds and connects clusters of galaxies. Comparing the maps generated by Roman to observations of the infant universe will allow scientists to study how things have changed over time.

“We're trying to answer fundamental questions about the universe, and it turns out to be incredibly challenging to do that,” Mandelbaum says. “We need really powerful observatories like Roman."

Addressing Cosmic Mysteries

In recent years, three notable aberrations have cropped up in the study of cosmology. The first is that the universe appears to be expanding faster today than it should be, according to models based on the conditions shortly after the Big Bang. The second is that the universe’s matter is distributed more evenly than expected.

And the third is a surprising recent find from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) in Arizona that suggests dark energy, the force driving the expansion of the universe, may be unexpectedly weakening over time.

These three tensions, as scientists call them, each point to an area where the standard model of cosmology may be missing key details.

“It's kind of tantalizing, because there's hints that something is very wrong,” McEnery says.

For each of these unsolved mysteries, Roman will provide valuable data. Regarding the expansion rate of the universe, the space telescope is expected to capture tens of thousands of supernova explosions, several times as many as have been observed so far. Certain supernovae can be used to measure the expansion rate of the universe today, meaning Roman will allow researchers to calculate this value more accurately.

The observatory’s maps of large-scale structures will also give researchers a better sense of the universe’s matter distribution, or clumpiness. And its measurements of dark matter’s gravitational effects will provide a detailed picture of how these structures have grown over time, allowing scientists to test whether the strength of dark energy truly has been changing as DESI suggests.

If it has, “we're pretty much guaranteed to be able to confirm what they're seeing, because it's exactly the thing we were designed to do,” McEnery says.

Roman’s vast view of the universe will reveal countless new details, and as scientists put the immense puzzle together, they may revolutionize our understanding of cosmology.

“We had a major breakthrough in the last century on the very small with the development of quantum mechanics and the discovery of elementary particles,” McEnery says. “Maybe this is the century of understanding the very big.”

entries.title: Asus ROG Swift RGB Stripe OLED Review: Clarity King
entries.summary: The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.
entries.content:
The Asus PG27UCWM brings a new sub-pixel layout to the world of OLED gaming monitors, and in my testing, I appreciated the improvements it brings to the table.

Top-notch contrast. Outstanding color performance. Crisp motion clarity. Absolutely loaded with extra features.

TIRED

Mirror-like display finish isn’t for everyone. Stand takes up a lot of space on the desk. Expensive at full price.

RGB Stripe OLED panels are the new hotness in 2026. The new OLED panel technology is designed to improve text clarity and color performance, which potentially give a monitor like the ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM a broader appeal beyond just a typical gaming monitor.

That is, perhaps, why Asus takes the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach. At a glance, it might seem like a typical 4K OLED gaming monitor. It has a 26.5-inch tandem 4K RGB Stripe OLED panel, a 240Hz refresh rate, and HDR support with VESA DisplayHDR 400 True Black certification. But it's also rounded out with tons of features, which helps make the higher price of $1,200 easier to swallow.

Super Glossy, Superior Contrast

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM has the company’s unique TrueBlack display finish, which is designed to deliver an ultrahigh-contrast experience in a wide variety of lighting conditions. It does so with a high-gloss coat that minimizes the impact of ambient light across the display.

It’s not just marketing drivel. The TrueBlack finish provides noticeably deeper black levels in a bright room. The matte OLED finish on Samsung’s OLEDs looks positively hazy by comparison. Glossy OLED monitors from competing brands also look less contrast-rich, though the difference is most noticeable in a very bright room—brighter, I suspect, than most PC gaming dens.

I also feel it comes across in how colors present. Technically, the monitor’s results are modest for an OLED monitor: It has a color gamut that spanned 94 percent of DCI-P3 and 89 percent of AdobeRGB. That’s a tad more narrow than top QD-OLED monitors, which can hit up to 98 percent and 95 percent, respectively. However, the ultra-clear, high-contrast look of the panel amplifies the sense of impact. I’m not saying it’s better than the best competitors, but the PG27UCWM’s overall image quality is in the upper tier. That's at least partially due to the fact that RGB Stripe OLED also improves “color volume," which is a display's ability to maintain color that gamut had max brightness.

Unfortunately, the vivid and contrast-rich image is paired with mirror-like reflections. I could likely use the monitor to shave. It’s not a problem in a dark room, but it’s noticeable when even modest ambient light is present.

This is an important, and divisive, point. Many OLED purists adore an ultra-gloss finish because it highlights the rich contrast and color the technology can provide. Others, myself included, prefer matte displays that reduce or eliminate discernible reflections.

There’s no right answer to this question, but you’ll need to decide your preference before you make a purchase.

Great for Sharpness, Great HDR

Beneath the PG27UCWM’s glossy coat you’ll find a tandem RGB Stripe OLED panel with a native resolution of 3840 x 2160. It’s crisp. Earlier OLED monitors have used an unusual sub-pixel arrangement that could hurt image clarity, but the PG27UCWM has a more conventional RGB sub-pixel layout that eliminates the issue. You'll sometimes see this marketed as “5th-Gen QD-OLED," and it initially launched in 34-inch monitors like the Alienware AW3426DW. But finally, the PG27UCWM is bringing it to the more standard 27-inch size.

Text clarity, in particular, has always been one of the chief issues about those shopping for OLED monitors, and I no longer have complaints in that regard. The resolution helps, too, providing a pixel density of about 165 pixels per inch across the 26.5-inch panel. The panel’s sharpness was excellent with the monitor connected to both my Windows 11 desktop and my MacBook Air M4.

HDR is where the PG27UCWM’s tandem OLED panel really begins to earn its keep. My testing found it can hit up to 800 nits of brightness. While that’s not a record-setting result, it’s in line with other premium OLED monitors, which typically offer 800 to 900 nits in my testing (the best barely clear 1,000 nits). The monitor also supports Dolby Vision HDR, which is rare.

The PG27UCWM’s brightness, contrast, and resolution combine to deliver real impact in HDR games. It’s so bright that it can at times feel overwhelming. Fortunately, Asus includes HDR brightness adjustment options that let you tone down the brightness if you’d prefer.

Asus’ PG27UCWM isn’t uniquely bright in HDR though. The Alienware AW3426DW, Acer Predator X27 X1, and MSI MPG 32URXW are among the monitors I’ve tested that deliver similar HDR brightness (and some of which are significantly cheaper). Still, the PG27UCWM performs much better than least expensive OLED monitors like the entry-level Alienware AW2726DM, which can only deliver roughly 400 nits in HDR.

Motion Clarity Checks the Boxes

The PG27UCWM can reach a refresh rate of up to 240 Hz at 4K resolution. That’s standard for a high-end 4K OLED in 2026. It also provides a dual-mode feature that can reduce the resolution to 1080p in exchange for a refresh rate of up to 480 Hz. That’s less common, though many OLED monitors now offer a similar feature.

I think the 1080p/480Hz mode will prove niche, as the monitor’s motion clarity is already excellent at 4K and 240 Hz. Motion blur is minimal and small objects are easy to make out. Though perhaps most useful in games, the monitor’s motion clarity is also noticeable on a Windows 11 or macOS desktop. Scrolling text is readable and OS animations look ultrasmooth.

Still, the 480 Hz mode has uses. It’s ideal for people who like to play competitively in esports titles, yet also want to enjoy maximum image quality in single-player games. The PG27UCWM can handle both without compromise.

The PG27UCWM lists compatibility with AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA Adaptive Sync. In practice, many monitors that list support for only one of these can work with all three, as they are based on the same core technology. However, I always prefer to see official support listed, so you don’t have to guess whether adaptive sync will work with your PC or game console.

Features Galore

The PG27UCWM is more than just excellent image quality though. Asus has packed it full with a treasure trove of features to sweeten the deal.

The monitor’s design is top-notch. It includes attractive transparent plastic elements on the rear of the display and an RGB-LED logo that can be synced to other RGB-LED devices with Asus’ Aura Sync. An ergonomic stand is included and offers the usual range of adjustment for height, tilt, swivel, and pivot; VESA mounting for third-party arms and stands is possible with a provided adapter.

There’s also an 1/4-inch screw mount on the top of the stand neck. This is a common type of mount for camera and streaming equipment. You can use the mount to place a webcam or ring light above the monitor. It’s an uncommon but useful feature.

I do have one nitpick with the stand, and that’s the stand base. Asus opts for a wide base that takes up a lot of desk space. It’s not the largest I’ve seen, but I prefer the more compact stand base found with competitors like the MSI MPG 272URX and Alienware AW2725Q. On the plus side, though, the stand is remarkably solid. Most monitor stands allow a hint of wobble if I purposefully jostle my desk, but the PG27UCWM is unbothered.

Image-quality purists will be happy to see the monitor is packed with adjustments. These include multiple color space presets, color temperature and gamma modes that target precise values, and six-axis color saturation adjustment.

The monitor even has a built-in sensor that can detect ambient light and the user’s presence. This is used primarily to enable the monitor’s OLED burn-in reduction features, which can turn off the monitor automatically when you step away (if it’s not on, it won’t burn in).

Connectivity is great, too. The monitor has two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and one USB-C port with DisplayPort input for a total of four video inputs. All of the inputs can reach 4K at 240 Hz, and the DisplayPort 2.1 port offers UHBR20 data rates of up to 80Gbps, which means it can hit the 4K/240 Hz target without display stream compression.

The USB-C port offers 90 watts of power delivery for charging a connected laptop or tablet. A USB-C hub is included, as well, and provides three downstream USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 ports. The USB-A ports are accessible through the USB-C input or a USB-B input. A KVM switch is present as well. As if that wasn't all, Asus even throws in a three-year warranty for good measure.

What’s the Catch?

The Asus ROG Swift OLED PG27UCWM is a great gaming monitor with a long list of features. It has a beautiful, sharp image, smooth-motion clarity, good HDR, lots of display inputs, and a USB hub. It even looks nice on a desk. The super-vivid, super-reflective TrueBlack coat won’t be to everyone’s taste, but it delivers on its promise to improve perceived contrast.

Which brings us to the only serious issue with the PG27UCWM: the price.

The monitor will set you back $1,200 at retail price. That’s a lot of clams for a 27-inch 4K OLED monitor. The PG27UCWM does a lot to justify a higher price, but I can’t broadly recommend the PG27UCWM over less expensive options like the PG27UCDM (currently $950) or MSI MPG 272URX (currently $800). Neither of those have the newer RGB Stripe OLED, of course, but that might not be enough for the average gamer to full appreciate given the hundreds of dollars of difference in price.

Still, the PG27UCWM is worth consideration if you want a flagship 27-inch 4K OLED monitor with the latest panel technology and a boatload of features when it becomes available in October. A 32-inch model will also be launched alongside it.

entries.title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026? (So Far)
entries.summary: I’ve tested every single Kindle. Here’s how Amazon’s ebook readers stack up.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.

I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.

Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Updated August 2026: The second-generation Kindle Scribe has been updated to be our pick for students, and prices have been updated throughout.

Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

Model Display Resolution Color? Storage Weight Battery life Waterproof
Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 pixels per inch (ppi) No 16 GB 7.4 ounces Up to 12 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Scribe (2024, 2nd Gen) 10.2 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi No 16, 32, or 64 GB 15.3 ounces Up to 12 weeks No
Kindle Colorsoft (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (Black-and-White), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 7.6 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (2024) 7 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 32 GB 7.7 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Kids (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 11.8 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) 6 inches, adjustable front light 300 ppi No 16 GB 5.56 ounces Up to 6 weeks No

What About the New Kindle Scribes?

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

Accessories for Easier Reading

If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

Cases and Covers

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs.

Looking for more accessory ideas? Check out my guide to all of the best Kindle accessories. Also, don't forget that if the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.

About Those Older Kindles

Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.

FAQs

Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?

As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.

The following Kindle devices are impacted:

  • Kindle 1st Generation
  • Kindle 2nd Generation
  • Kindle DX
  • Kindle DX Graphite
  • Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
  • Kindle 4
  • Kindle Touch
  • Kindle 5
  • Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation

What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?

Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.

Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.

How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?

If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.

If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.

If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:

  • Get a library card for your local branch.
  • Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
  • Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.

If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.

What Else Can a Kindle Do?

Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.

Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations, and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.

While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.

When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.

Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.

There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.

How Do You Update a Kindle?

When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.

What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?

Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.

Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?

The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.

You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.

Are Kindles Good for Students?

Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.
